title: Wren v. Columbia St. Mary’s Hospital
description: Whether Wisconsin Statute § 895.4801, which grants immunity to health care professionals during the COVID-19 pandemic, facially violates the constitutional right to a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the immunity statute is unconstitutional because it deprives litigants of their fundamental right to a jury trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the immunity statute is constitutional, as the legislature has the power to suspend common law causes of action, and therefore, no jury trial right attaches.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' decision, holding that Wisconsin Statute § 895.4801 does not facially violate the constitutional right to a jury trial because the legislature has the power to abrogate common law causes of action, and without a cause of action, the right to a jury trial does not attach.

title: State v. Ramirez
description: Whether Luis A. Ramirez's constitutional right to a speedy trial was violated by a 46-month delay between being charged and convicted.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Ramirez's constitutional right to a speedy trial was not violated, as the delays were attributable to valid or neutral reasons, and Ramirez failed to assert his right promptly or show particularized prejudice.
defendant_argument: Ramirez argued that the 46-month delay violated his constitutional speedy trial right, causing him prejudice due to restricted status and stress-related health issues.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that Ramirez's constitutional right to a speedy trial was not violated and reversed the court of appeals' decision to dismiss the charges, remanding the case to the circuit court.

title: Wisconsin State Legislature v. Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction
description: Whether the governor's partial veto of S.B. 971 was constitutional, and whether the Joint Committee on Finance (JCF) improperly withheld funds earmarked for literacy programs from the Department of Public Instruction (DPI).
plaintiff_argument: The Wisconsin State Legislature argued that the governor's partial veto of S.B. 971 was unconstitutional because it was not an appropriation bill, and that JCF properly withheld funds from DPI as the money was appropriated to JCF, not DPI.
defendant_argument: The governor and DPI argued that S.B. 971 was an appropriation bill subject to the governor's partial veto authority, and that JCF improperly withheld the $50 million earmarked for literacy programs from DPI, contending JCF lacked discretion to withhold these funds.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the governor's partial veto of S.B. 971 was unconstitutional because it was not an appropriation bill, and affirmed that JCF did not improperly withhold funds from DPI.

title: Josh Kaul v. Wisconsin State Legislature
description: Whether a state law requiring the Joint Finance Committee's approval for the Department of Justice to settle certain civil cases (civil enforcement actions and cases brought at executive-branch agencies' request) violates the Wisconsin Constitution's separation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (DOJ, Attorney General, Governor) argues that settling civil enforcement actions and cases brought at the request of executive-branch agencies constitutes core executive power, and the Legislature's requirement for JFC approval unconstitutionally interferes with this power.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Wisconsin State Legislature) argues that the power to settle these cases is a shared power, not exclusively executive, and that it has constitutional institutional interests in the power of the purse and in setting public policy, justifying its approval requirement.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the statutory requirement for JFC approval for the Department of Justice to settle civil enforcement actions and agency-requested cases violates the Wisconsin Constitution's separation of powers, reversing the court of appeals and affirming the circuit court's decision.

title: Planned Parenthood v. Urmanski
description: Whether the Wisconsin Supreme Court should proceed with an original action filed by Planned Parenthood to establish a constitutional right to abortion, or dismiss it based on a related statutory interpretation case.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argues for the court to establish a constitutional right to abortion through this original action.
defendant_argument: The respondents (district attorneys) implicitly argue against the original action proceeding, and the court's decision to dismiss aligns with this.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the original action filed by Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin et al.

title: Kaul v. Urmanski
description: Whether Wisconsin Statute § 940.04(1), an 1849 law criminalizing the intentional destruction of an unborn child, still bans abortion, or if it has been impliedly repealed by subsequent comprehensive legislation.
plaintiff_argument: The 1849 statute either does not apply to abortion or has been impliedly repealed by numerous subsequent statutes regulating abortion, rendering a near-total ban meaningless.
defendant_argument: The plain language of the 1849 statute bans nearly all abortions, and the legislature has not impliedly repealed that prohibition.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, holding that the legislature impliedly repealed § 940.04(1) as to abortion, and therefore, the statute does not ban abortion in Wisconsin.

title: Evers v. Marklein
description: Whether statutes granting the Joint Committee for Review of Administrative Rules (JCRAR) the power to pause, object to, or suspend administrative rules are unconstitutional legislative vetoes, with the Governor arguing they are unconstitutional and the Legislature arguing they are permissible as an extension of legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor argued that the challenged statutes, which allow JCRAR to pause, object to, or suspend administrative rules, amount to unconstitutional legislative vetoes because they alter legal rights and duties outside the legislative branch without adhering to bicameralism and presentment requirements.
defendant_argument: The Legislature argued that the challenged statutes are permissible because rulemaking is an appropriate extension of legislative power, and JCRAR's actions are part of the Legislature's appropriate rulemaking oversight authority, not requiring bicameralism and presentment.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that all five challenged statutes, WIS. STAT. §§ 227.19(5)(c), (d), (dm), and 227.26(2)(d), (im), are facially unconstitutional because they violate the Wisconsin Constitution's bicameralism and presentment requirements.

title: LeMieux v. Evers
description: Whether Governor Tony Evers exceeded his partial veto authority under Article V, Section 10(1) of the Wisconsin Constitution by extending an education revenue limit increase from two fiscal years to 402 fiscal years through partial vetoes.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the governor's partial vetoes violated Article V, Section 10(1)(b) because extending a two-year duration to 402 years is not vetoing "in part" (as 402 is not less than 2), and violated Section 10(1)(c) by striking digits to create new numbers.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that the partial vetoes were constitutional, as they satisfied the established deletion-veto principles and did not violate the prohibition against creating new words by striking letters or creating new sentences.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the governor's 2023 partial vetoes were consistent with Article V Sections 10(1)(b) and (c) of the Wisconsin Constitution, denying the petitioners' requested relief.

title: Brown v. Wisconsin Elections Commission
description: Whether Kenneth Brown has standing to seek judicial review of a Wisconsin Elections Commission (WEC) decision regarding in-person absentee voting procedures, with Brown arguing he has standing due to injury to his statutory right to compliant election officials, and WEC arguing he lacks standing because he was not personally aggrieved by their decision.
plaintiff_argument: Brown contended that he has standing to seek judicial review because WEC's decision not to act on his complaint injured his statutory right to have local election officials comply with the law.
defendant_argument: WEC asserted that Brown does not have standing because he was not "aggrieved by an order" as he failed to demonstrate a personal injury to a legally recognized interest as a result of WEC's decision.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's decision, ruling that Kenneth Brown does not have standing to seek judicial review of the Wisconsin Elections Commission's decision, and remanded the case with instructions to dismiss.

title: State v. Hoyle
description: Whether a prosecutor's repeated characterization of evidence as "uncontroverted" during closing arguments violates a defendant's Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecutor's comments describing the State's evidence as "uncontroverted" were not intended to comment on the defendant's silence and therefore did not violate his Fifth Amendment rights.
defendant_argument: The prosecutor's comments that the evidence was "uncontroverted" implicitly commented on the defendant's decision not to testify, as only he could have contradicted the victim's testimony, thereby violating his Fifth Amendment rights.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that the prosecutor's comments did not violate the defendant's Fifth Amendment rights and reinstated the conviction.

title: Priorities USA v. Wisconsin Elections Commission
description: Whether to overrule the Court's holding in Teigen v. Wisconsin Elections Commission that Wis. Stat. § 6.87 precludes the use of secure drop boxes for the return of absentee ballots to municipal clerks, with the pro position arguing that drop boxes are allowed and the con position arguing they are precluded.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners, along with intervenor Governor Tony Evers and respondent WEC, contended that Teigen was wrongly decided and that Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1. allows the use of ballot drop boxes.
defendant_argument: The Wisconsin Legislature advanced that Teigen was correctly decided and should be reaffirmed, meaning the court's statutory interpretation in that case was correct and no intervening changes warranted revisiting the decision.
decision_outcome: The court overruled its previous holding in Teigen v. Wisconsin Elections Commission, concluding that Wis. Stat. § 6.87(4)(b)1. allows the use of ballot drop boxes, and reversed the circuit court's order dismissing the petitioners' claim.

title: Catholic Charities Bureau, Inc. v. State
description: Whether Catholic Charities Bureau, Inc. and its sub-entities are operated primarily for religious purposes to qualify for an unemployment tax exemption, and whether denying this exemption violates the First Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: Catholic Charities Bureau (CCB) argues they are operated primarily for religious purposes due to the Diocese's religious motivation and charitable works, and that denying the unemployment tax exemption violates the First Amendment's Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses.
defendant_argument: The Labor and Industry Review Commission (LIRC) argues that the organization's actual activities, not its motivations, determine if it is operated primarily for religious purposes, and its activities are secular, thus not qualifying for the exemption and not violating the First Amendment.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals' decision, ruling that Catholic Charities Bureau, Inc. and its sub-entities are not operated primarily for religious purposes and are therefore not exempt from unemployment tax, and that this application does not violate the First Amendment.

title: Wisconsin Property Taxpayers, Inc. v. Town of Buchanan
description: Whether the Transportation Utility Fee (TUF) imposed by the Town of Buchanan is a property tax subject to municipal levy limits under Wis. Stat. § 66.0602 and the Uniformity Clause of the Wisconsin Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Wisconsin Property Taxpayers, Inc. (WPT), argued that the TUF is a property tax subject to municipal levy limits and that the Town exceeded its levy limit by not offsetting the TUF revenue. WPT also contended that the TUF's assessment method, based on estimated road usage rather than property value, violates the Uniformity Clause.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Town of Buchanan, argued that Wis. Stat. § 66.0827 authorizes the TUF as a special tax, not a general property tax, and therefore it is not subject to municipal levy limits or the Uniformity Clause. The Town also claimed that the utility district funding supports a separate governmental unit, exempting it from the Town's general property tax levy.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's decision, holding that funds raised for utility districts under Wis. Stat. § 66.0827 are property taxes subject to municipal levy limits, and thus the Town unlawfully exceeded its levy limit by imposing the Transportation Utility Fee.

title: Clarke v. Wisconsin Elections Commission
description: Whether the current state legislative districts violate the Wisconsin Constitution's requirement that districts consist of contiguous territory.
plaintiff_argument: The current legislative districts are non-contiguous and violate the Wisconsin Constitution, and their adoption violated the separation of powers. They sought to enjoin the use of current maps, order remedial maps, and invalidate 2022 state senate elections with special elections.
defendant_argument: The current legislative districts comply with contiguity requirements, arguing that municipal islands are legally contiguous. They also argued that the petitioners lacked standing and their claims were barred by laches, preclusion, and estoppel, and that the requested relief was unavailable.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the current legislative districts violate the Wisconsin Constitution's contiguity requirements and enjoined the Wisconsin Elections Commission from using them in future elections, requiring new remedial maps to be drawn. However, the court declined to invalidate the results of the 2022 state senate elections or order special elections.

title: Teigen v. Wisconsin Elections Commission
description: Whether ballot drop boxes are legal under Wisconsin statutes and whether an agent of a voter may return an absentee ballot on the voter's behalf.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that WEC's documents authorizing ballot drop boxes and agent delivery of absentee ballots are invalid because they are unpromulgated administrative rules and violate Wisconsin statutes requiring personal delivery or mailing of absentee ballots directly by the voter to the municipal clerk.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that WEC's memos are valid guidance, not administrative rules, and that ballot drop boxes and agent delivery are permissible under Wisconsin statutes, with WEC providing guidance in response to clerks' inquiries.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's decision, declaring that WEC's authorization of ballot drop boxes was unlawful and that absentee ballots delivered in person must be delivered personally by the voter to the municipal clerk, not by an agent.

title: Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission
description: Whether the Wisconsin Supreme Court should grant a motion for relief from its prior decision and order concerning the adoption of congressional district maps.
plaintiff_argument: The intervenors-petitioners (Lisa Hunter et al.) argued that the court should grant relief from its previous decision regarding congressional district maps.
defendant_argument: The court, by denying the motion, implicitly argued that relief from its prior decision regarding congressional district maps should not be granted.
decision_outcome: The court denied the motion for relief from judgment.

title: State v. Johnson
description: Whether the Shiffra procedure, which allows criminal defendants to obtain in camera review of a victim's privately held, privileged health records, should be overruled.
plaintiff_argument: The State and the victim (T.A.J.) argued that the Shiffra procedure was wrongly decided, unworkable, and its rationale had been undermined by subsequent legal developments, thus it should be overruled.
defendant_argument: Johnson sought in camera review of T.A.J.'s mental health and counseling records, citing Shiffra, and argued that T.A.J. lacked standing to oppose the motion.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' decision and overruled Shiffra, denying Johnson's motion for in camera review of T.A.J.'s privately held, privileged mental health treatment records.

title: Wisconsin Justice Initiative,  Inc. v. Wisconsin Elections Commission
description: Whether the ballot question for Marsy's Law, which expanded victims' rights, was submitted to the people in a constitutionally compliant manner, specifically regarding its content and whether it should have been presented as multiple amendments.
plaintiff_argument: The ballot question failed to contain "every essential" of the proposed amendment, misled voters by neglecting its impact on criminal defendants' rights, and should have been submitted as multiple amendments.
defendant_argument: The legislature has broad discretion in submitting amendments, the ballot question was not fundamentally counterfactual, and all provisions of Marsy's Law relate to a single general purpose.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's judgment, concluding that Marsy's Law was validly ratified and the ballot question complied with constitutional requirements.

title: Becker v. Dane Cnty.
description: Whether the court should reconsider its previous decision that upheld the delegation of broad public health authority to local governments, where petitioners argue the court misapplied historical statutes to justify such delegation to unelected officials.
plaintiff_argument: The court's previous decision was based on a flawed historical analysis of the 1849 statute, which incorrectly found support for delegating broad lawmaking authority to unelected public health officials, thereby violating the nondelegation principle.
defendant_argument: The court's original decision was correct, its historical interpretation was sound, and the motion for reconsideration does not meet the standards for being granted.
decision_outcome: The court denied the plaintiffs' motion for reconsideration, upholding its previous decision regarding the nondelegation principle.

title: State v. Moeser
description: Whether a search warrant for a blood draw was constitutionally defective because the affiant was not placed under oath or affirmation, with the plaintiff arguing the requirement was met by the affiant's intent and the defendant arguing the omission made the warrant invalid.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the oath or affirmation requirement was met because Sergeant Brown manifested the intent to be bound by his statement, even without a formal oral oath.
defendant_argument: Moeser argued that the warrant was constitutionally defective because Sergeant Brown was not placed under oath or affirmation when signing the affidavit, failing to satisfy Fourth Amendment requirements.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals' decision, denying Moeser's motion to suppress the blood test evidence.

title: Doe v. Madison Metropolitan School District
description: Whether parents challenging a school district's gender identity policy can proceed with full anonymity, specifically withholding their identities from the school district's attorneys, and whether the court should address the merits of the underlying policy at this stage.
plaintiff_argument: The parents argued that their identities should be fully sealed and confidential from the public and the school district's attorneys due to risks of harassment and retaliation, and that their identities are irrelevant to their constitutional claims regarding parental rights over their children's upbringing and education.
defendant_argument: The school district argued that withholding the parents' identities from their attorneys was unwarranted, as attorneys are duty-bound to confidentiality and knowing the parents' identities is necessary to assess potential conflicts of interest and develop legal defenses based on the unique circumstances of each parent.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals' decision, which upheld the circuit court's ruling to allow parents to proceed pseudonymously to the public and the school district, but required disclosure of their identities to the school district's attorneys. The court declined to address the merits of the underlying policy or grant injunctive relief at this stage, deeming it moot or not properly before them.

title: State ex rel. Kaul v. Prehn
description: Whether Frederick Prehn lawfully holds his position on the Wisconsin Board of Natural Resources after his term expired and whether he can be removed without cause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (State/Attorney General) argued that Prehn's term expiration created a vacancy, he unlawfully holds office, and he can be removed at the Governor's pleasure without cause.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Prehn) argued that no vacancy occurred upon his term's expiration, he lawfully remains as a holdover until a successor is confirmed, and he is entitled to "for cause" protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's decision, ruling that Prehn lawfully retains his position as a holdover and can only be removed for cause, not at the Governor's pleasure, and dismissed the State's complaint.

title: James v. Heinrich
description: Whether a local health officer has the statutory authority to issue an emergency order closing schools for in-person instruction and whether such an order violates fundamental constitutional rights, specifically the free exercise of religion.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the emergency order exceeded the local health officer's statutory authority and violated their fundamental rights to the free exercise of religion and parents' rights to direct their children's education.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that local health officers have the statutory authority to issue school closure orders and that the emergency order is constitutional under established precedent or does not violate the Wisconsin Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the local health officer lacked statutory authority to close schools and that the emergency order violated the petitioners' fundamental right to the free exercise of religion, thus vacating the order.

title: State v. VanBeek
description: Whether a consensual encounter becomes an unconstitutional seizure under the Fourth Amendment when an officer requests and takes an individual's driver's license to the officer's squad car without reasonable suspicion.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that VanBeek was not seized when the officer took her driver's license, or if she was seized, it occurred later and was supported by reasonable suspicion.
defendant_argument: VanBeek argued that she was unlawfully seized when the officer took her driver's license back to his squad car, as a reasonable person would not feel free to leave, and this seizure lacked reasonable suspicion.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment of conviction and remanded with instructions to grant VanBeek's motion to suppress.

title: State v. Halverson
description: Whether an incarcerated individual is per se in custody for Miranda purposes, with the plaintiff arguing against a per se rule and the defendant arguing for it, either under a per se rule or the totality of circumstances.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Brian L. Halverson was not in custody for Miranda purposes during the phone interview, rejecting a per se rule for incarcerated individuals and asserting that the totality of circumstances did not warrant Miranda warnings.
defendant_argument: Brian L. Halverson argued that his statements should be suppressed because he was in custody as an inmate in jail, either under a per se rule for incarcerated individuals or under the traditional Miranda custody test based on the totality of circumstances.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals' decision, concluding that Brian L. Halverson was not "in custody" for Miranda purposes during the phone interview and therefore his motion to suppress his statements should have been denied.
